summary: Provides the initial Management Information Base (MIB) for managing TCP/IP-based internets in the short term. It works with companion memos on the structure of management information and the management protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1156.

eli5.summary: This is the first list of what you can ask a network device about, like its name or how many packets it has handled.

questions: what is the management information base for tcp/ip
subtitle: The first standard set of network management objects for TCP/IP systems.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP network operators needed a standard way to query network devices for status and statistics, but had no defined set of managed objects.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) containing essential objects organized into eight groups: System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, and EGP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1066 was replaced by RFC 1156, which provides an improved version of the same MIB specification.

facts.label: Object groups
facts.value: 8 (System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP)

today: RFC 1066 has been replaced by RFC 1156, which provides an improved version of the Management Information Base with refinements and additional objects for TCP/IP network management.

sections.title: Introduction and Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 1066 provides the first standard Management Information Base (MIB) for managing TCP/IP networks. It works together with a companion memo that defines the Structure for Management Information (SMI, defined in RFC 1065) and uses the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) to retrieve and set these managed objects.

The MIB takes a practical approach: instead of defining hundreds of optional objects, it specifies only essential objects that every compliant implementation must support. If a device implements a particular protocol or function (such as TCP), it must implement all objects in that function's group. This design makes it easier for vendors to fully instrument their software with just about 100 core objects.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a standard questionnaire for network devices. It says: if you have TCP, you must answer these 10 questions about TCP. If you have UDP, you must answer these questions about UDP. Everyone uses the same form.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Object Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is organized into eight groups, each containing related management objects:

System Group: Mandatory for all systems. Contains basic information like the device description, an object identifier for the device type, and the time since the management portion was last reinitialized.

Interfaces Group: Mandatory for all systems. Describes each network interface on the device, including its type (Ethernet, serial, etc.), maximum transmission unit (MTU), speed estimate, physical address, administrative and operational status, and traffic counters (octets and packets in and out, errors, discards).

Address Translation Group: Mandatory for all systems. Contains mappings between network addresses (such as IP addresses) and the physical addresses used by underlying networks (such as MAC addresses in ARP caches).

IP Group: Mandatory for systems implementing IP. Includes IP configuration and routing information, including routing tables that specify how to forward packets to different destinations.

ICMP Group: Contains statistics for the Internet Control Message Protocol, such as counts of echo requests and echo replies.

TCP Group: Mandatory for systems implementing TCP. Provides connection statistics and parameters, including a table of active TCP connections.

UDP Group: Mandatory for systems implementing UDP. Contains UDP connection information and statistics.

EGP Group: Mandatory for gateways using the Exterior Gateway Protocol. Contains information about neighbors and protocol exchanges.
sections.eli5: The MIB organizes objects into groups: System stuff (name, uptime), Interface stuff (how fast, how many packets), and stuff for each protocol like TCP and UDP. You must support a group if you run that protocol.

sections.title: Objects and Data Types
sections.content:
Each managed object in the MIB has a name (object identifier), an abstract syntax (its data type), a human-readable description, an access level, and a status. Objects use ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) for their type definitions, but the MIB restricts ASN.1 to simple types for implementation simplicity.

Common data types include:

OCTET STRING: A sequence of bytes, used for text descriptions and physical addresses. Must contain only printable ASCII characters when used for human-readable information.

INTEGER: Represents whole numbers, often with defined ranges or named values (like interface types: ethernet(6), token-ring(9), etc.).

Counter: A non-negative integer that increments monotonically and wraps around. Used for cumulative statistics like packet counts.

Gauge: A non-negative integer that can increase or decrease. Used for values like the current queue length or interface speed.

TimeTicks: Represents time in hundredths of a second, used for measuring elapsed time.

Each object also specifies access level: read-only (for statistics and status), read-write (for configuration), or not-accessible (for internal structure).
sections.eli5: Each question you can ask a device has a name, a type of answer (number, text, etc.), and whether the device is allowed to let you change it. Most statistics are read-only; some settings are read-write.

sections.title: Key Objects and Examples
sections.content:
The System group illustrates the approach. sysDescr is a text description including the device's full name and version. sysObjectID is an object identifier that uniquely identifies the device manufacturer and model, assigned within the SMI enterprises subtree. sysUpTime reports how long the device has been operational in hundredths of a second.

The Interfaces group provides extensive detail. ifNumber counts how many interfaces exist. ifTable is a table with one row per interface. Each row includes: ifIndex (unique interface number), ifDescr (text description), ifType (ethernet, serial, etc.), ifMtu (maximum transmission unit in octets), and ifSpeed (estimated bandwidth in bits per second).

Counters track traffic: ifInOctets (total bytes received), ifInUcastPkts (unicast packets received), ifInNUcastPkts (broadcast or multicast packets received), ifInErrors (packets with errors), and ifInUnknownProtos (packets with unknown protocol types). Corresponding outbound counters track transmitted traffic.

The IP group includes a routing table that specifies the next hop for reaching different destinations, allowing operators to verify that routing is configured correctly.
sections.eli5: A device can tell you its name and model, how long it has been running, how many network interfaces it has, and for each one: its type, speed, and statistics like total bytes sent and received, and how many errors happened.

sections.title: Design Philosophy and Extensibility
sections.content:
RFC 1066 reflects a deliberate minimalist design. The specification includes only objects that meet strict criteria: they must be essential for fault or configuration management, they must exist in all referenced prior MIB definitions or be demonstrably essential, they must have evidence of practical use, and implementation-specific objects (such as BSD-specific fields) are excluded. This approach keeps vendor implementation effort reasonable while providing all necessary monitoring capabilities.

The design intentionally avoids redundancy: objects that can be derived from others are not included. For example, you do not need a separate object for inbound multicast percentage because you can calculate it from the existing packet counts.

Extensibility is built in. The SMI defines three extensibility mechanisms: new standard objects can be added in future MIB versions, vendor-specific objects can be added in the enterprises subtree (1.3.6.1.4.1), and experimental objects can be added for testing. This allows the MIB to grow as needs evolve without breaking existing implementations.
sections.eli5: The designers chose only the most important things you might want to know, and avoided asking for information twice or for things specific to one company. They also left room to add new questions later as technology changes.
